**(Surah Al-Asr)**
Three verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By time,﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿By time,﴾ Know that they mentioned several opinions regarding the interpretation of *al-'asr* (time/afternoon):

The first: that it is *al-dahr* (eternity/the course of time). The proponent of this view argued with several points:

One of them: what has been narrated "from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he swore by *al-dahr*," and "he (peace be upon him) used to recite: *Wa al-'asr, wa nawa'ib al-dahr* (By time, and the calamities of time)." However, we say: this would invalidate the prayer, so we do not say that he recited it as Qur'an, but as an explanation (*tafsir*). Perhaps God, exalted is He, did not mention *al-dahr* because He knew that the atheist is fond of mentioning and glorifying it. For this reason He mentioned it in: ﴿Has there come upon man?﴾ [al-Insan: 1], as a refutation of the corruption of their saying that it is nature and time (*al-dahr*).

Second: *al-dahr* contains wonders, for in it occur happiness and hardship, health and sickness, wealth and poverty. Indeed, in it is something more wondrous than every wonder: that the intellect cannot prevail upon it to judge it as non-existent, for it is divided and partitioned into years, months, days and hours, and is described with increase, decrease, correspondence, and being past and future. How, then, could it be non-existent? Nor can one judge it to be existent, because the present is not divisible, while the past and future are both non-existent. So how is it possible to judge it as existent?

Third: the remaining life of a person has no value. If you wasted a thousand years and then repented in the last moment of your life, you would remain in Paradise forever. Then you would know that the most noble of things is your life in that moment. Thus time and eternity are among the fundamental blessings, and for this reason He swore by it and drew attention to the fact that night and day are an opportunity which the responsible person wastes. To this He alludes in His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day successive for whoever wishes to remember or wishes gratitude﴾ [al-Furqan: 62].

Fourth: His saying, exalted is He, in Surah al-An'am: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 12], indicates place and what is in place. Then He said: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾ [al-An'am: 13], which indicates time and what is in time. We have already explained there that time is higher and more noble than place. Since this is so, swearing by *al-'asr* is swearing by the nobler of the two halves of the dominion of Allah and His kingdom.

Fifth: they used to attribute loss to the calamities of time. So it is as if He, exalted is He, swore that time and *al-'asr* are a blessing with no defect in them; the loser who is blamed is only man.

Sixth: He, exalted is He, mentioned *al-'asr*, by whose passing your life is diminished. If there is no gain in exchange for it, that diminution becomes nothing but loss. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed we rejoice in the days as we pass them, but every day that passes is a decrease from the term."*

So the meaning is: "By the wondrous time, whose matter is such that man rejoices in its passing, thinking he has found profit, while in fact it is the demolition of his life; and indeed he is in loss."

The second opinion, which is the opinion of Abu Muslim: the intended meaning of *al-'asr* is one of the two ends of the day. The reasons for this are several:

One of them: He, exalted is He, swore by *al-'asr* as He swore by *ad-duha* (the forenoon), because both contain signs of power. Every morning is like the Resurrection: people come out of their graves, the dead become living, and the scales are set up. Every evening resembles the destruction of the world by the thunderbolt and death. Each of these two states is a witness of justice. Then, if the judge does not rule following the two witnesses, he is considered a loser. Likewise, the person heedless of these two is in loss.

Second: al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He only swore by this time to alert that the markets are nearing the time of their closing and the end of trade and earning in them. If you did not earn, and you entered the house while your dependents circled around you, each one asking you for what is his due, then you would be ashamed and you would be among the losers. Likewise we say: *wa al-'asr*, i.e., the time of this world, the Resurrection has drawn near, and you have not yet prepared yourself. You know that tomorrow you will be asked about the blessings you enjoyed in your worldly life, and you will be asked about your dealings with creation. Every oppressed person will claim what is due to him from you; then you are a loser. A parallel to this is: ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near to them while they are heedless and turn away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1].

Third: this time is glorified, and the evidence for this is his (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever swears falsely after the 'asr prayer, Allah will not speak to him, nor look at him on the Day of Resurrection." Just as He swore by *ad-duha* concerning the one who gains, so He swore by *al-'asr* concerning the one who loses. This is because He swore by *ad-duha* concerning the winner, and the Messenger gave glad tidings that his affair is toward advancement; here, concerning the loser, He threatened him that his affair is toward regression. Then it is as if He says: "Some of the day remains," urging him to make up for what is left by repentance. It is reported from one of the early generations (*salaf*): "I learned the meaning of the surah from an ice seller. He would shout: 'Have mercy on one whose capital is melting! Have mercy on one whose capital is melting!' I said: This is the meaning of: ﴿Indeed, man is in loss﴾. The afternoon passes over him, his life goes by, and he has not earned; so he is a loser."

The third opinion: the opinion of Muqatil: He intended the *'asr* prayer. They mentioned several points regarding this:

One of them: He, exalted is He, swore by the 'asr prayer because of its excellence, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], which is the 'asr prayer in the codex of Hafsah. It has also been said that His saying: ﴿You detain them after the prayer, and they swear by Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106] refers to the 'asr prayer.

Second: his (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever misses the 'asr prayer, it is as if he has lost his family and his wealth."

Third: the obligation to perform it is more difficult, because people are busy with their trades and earnings at the end of the day and occupied with their livelihoods.

Fourth: it has been narrated that "a woman used to cry out in the streets of Madinah, saying: 'Direct me to the Prophet (ﷺ)!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw her and asked her what had happened. She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my husband was away from me, so I committed adultery, and a child was born to me from the fornication. I put the child in a jar of vinegar until it died. Then we sold that vinegar. Is there any repentance for me?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'As for adultery, the penalty for you is stoning. As for killing the child, its recompense is Hell. As for selling the vinegar, you have committed a great sin. However, I think you have abandoned the 'asr prayer.'" In this hadith there is an indication of the magnification of the affair of this prayer.

Fifth: the 'asr prayer completes the acts of worship of the day, so it is like repentance, by which deeds are concluded. Just as repentance is obligatory to be enjoined, so also the 'asr prayer, because matters are judged by their conclusions. He therefore swore by this prayer, magnifying its status, increasing the exhortation of the responsible person to perform it, and indicating that if you perform it properly, your loss will become gain, as He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾.

Sixth: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Three whom Allah will not look at on the Day of Resurrection, nor speak to, nor purify, and among them is a man who swears falsely after the 'asr prayer."

(If it is said): the 'asr prayer is our act, so how is it permissible to say that Allah, exalted is He, swore by it?

The answer: it is not an oath because it is our act, but because it is a noble matter by which Allah, exalted is He, has made us worship Him.

The fourth opinion: that it is an oath by the time of the Messenger (peace be upon him). They argued for this with his (peace be upon him) saying: "The example of you and of those before you is like a man who hired a worker and said: 'Who will work from dawn until noon for a qirat?' The Jews worked. Then he said: 'Who will work from noon until the 'asr for a qirat?' The Christians worked. Then he said: 'Who will work from the 'asr until sunset for two qirats?' You worked. The Jews and Christians became angry and said: 'We did more work and received less pay!' Allah said: 'Have I deprived you of anything of your wage?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will. You were fewer in work and greater in reward.'" This report indicates that *al-'asr* is the time specific to him and to his community. Therefore Allah swore by it. So His saying ﴿By time﴾ means: "By the time in which you are." Thus He swore by his time in this verse, by his place in His saying: ﴿And you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], and by his life in His saying: ﴿By your life﴾ [al-Hijr: 72]. It is as if He said: "By your time, your city, and your life," and all of that is like a container for him. If the status of the container must be magnified, then consider the status of what is contained. Then He directed the oath as if saying: "You, O Muhammad, came to them and called them, and they turned away from you and did not pay attention to you. How great is their loss, and how grave is their abandonment."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 103, verse 2:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾. In it are several issues:

The first issue: The alif and lam in "al-insan" (mankind) may be for the genus (jins), or for a previously known specific referent (al-ma'hud al-sabiq). Therefore the exegetes gave two opinions on it.

The first: that what is meant by it is the genus, as in the saying "the dirham has become abundant in people's hands." What supports this view is the exception of "those who believe" from "mankind."

The second view: what is meant is a specific individual. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means a group of polytheists, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abu Lahab. In a marfu' report it is said that it was Abu Jahl. It is narrated that these people used to say: "Indeed Muhammad is in loss," so Exalted is He swore that the matter is the opposite of what they imagined.

The second issue: al-khusr (loss) is al-khusran (losing), as it is said: "disbelief" (al-kufr) is in "ingratitude" (al-kufran). Its meaning is deficiency and the going of the capital (ra's al-mal). Then there are two interpretations of it, because if we take "mankind" as the genus, the meaning of loss is the ruin of one's self and one's life, except for the believer who acts righteously, for his life and wealth are not ruined, because by them he has gained everlasting happiness. If we take the word "mankind" to refer to the disbeliever, the meaning is his being in misguidance and disbelief, except for those among them who believe; then he is delivered from that loss to profit.

The third issue: He said ﴿in loss﴾ and did not say "in the loss," because indefiniteness (al-tankir) conveys magnification (al-tahwil) at times and belittlement (al-tahqir) at others. If we take it in the first sense, the meaning is that mankind is in a great loss whose reality none knows but God. Its explanation is that sin grows in magnitude according to the greatness of the one against whom the sin is committed, or because it occurs in opposition to great blessings. Both aspects are present in the servant's sin against his Lord, so that sin is necessarily of the utmost greatness. If we take it in the second sense, the meaning is that the loss of mankind is less than the loss of Satan, and in this there is good news that among My creation there is one more disobedient than you. The correct interpretation is the first.

The fourth issue: One might say: His saying ﴿in loss﴾ conveys singularity, although it encompasses kinds of loss.

The answer: the true loss is his being deprived of serving his Lord. As for the rest, namely being deprived of Paradise and falling into the Fire, these are, in relation to the first, as nothing. This is like how mankind in his existence has benefits; then He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. That is, since this purpose is the most exalted of purposes, all other purposes are, relative to it, as nothing.

Know that God, Exalted is He, joined to this verse indicators that point to His emphasis in explaining that mankind is in loss:

One: His saying ﴿in loss﴾ conveys that he is as one submerged in loss, and that it has encompassed him from every side.

Second: the word "inna" (indeed), for it is for emphasis.

Third: the letter lam in ﴿la-fi khusr﴾.

Here there are two possibilities:

The first: in His saying ﴿in loss﴾, meaning "on the path of loss," like His saying concerning consuming the property of orphans: ﴿They only consume into their bellies fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], since its outcome is the Fire.

The second possibility: that mankind does not cease from loss, because loss is the squandering of the capital, and his capital is his life, and he rarely escapes squandering his life. This is because every hour that passes over a person: if it is spent in disobedience, there is no doubt of loss; and if it is occupied with permissible things, loss is also present, because, as it has gone, no trace of it remains, although he was able to do in it an action whose trace would remain forever. And if it is occupied with acts of obedience, there is no act of obedience except that it is possible to perform it, or something else, in a better manner than that, because the degrees of humility and submissiveness toward God are unlimited, for the degrees of God's majesty and dominion are unlimited. Whenever a person's knowledge of them is greater, his fear of Him, Exalted is He, is greater, so his glorification when performing acts of obedience is more complete and perfect. Leaving the higher and settling for the lower is a kind of loss. Thus it is established that mankind never fully escapes some kind of loss.

Know that this verse is like an alert that the default state of mankind is to be in loss and failure. Its explanation: the happiness of mankind lies in love of the Hereafter and turning away from this world. Then the causes that call to the Hereafter are hidden, while the causes that call to love of this world are manifest, namely the five senses, desire, and anger. For this reason most of creation became occupied with love of this world, absorbed in seeking it, and so they were in loss and ruin.

If it is said: He, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Tin: ﴿Indeed, We created mankind in the best stature﴾, ﴿then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 4-5]. There it indicates that the beginning is from perfection and the end is toward deficiency, while here it indicates that the beginning is from deficiency and the end is toward perfection. So how is the reconciliation?

We say: what is mentioned in Surat al-Tin concerns the states of the body, while here it concerns the states of the soul, so there is no contradiction between the two statements.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 103, verse 3:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾.

Know that faith (iman) and righteous deeds have already been explained many times before. Then, here, there are several questions.

**The first question:** Those who hold that deeds are not part of the definition of faith argue that God Most High joined the doing of righteous deeds to faith with a conjunction. If the doing of righteous deeds were included in the meaning of faith, that would be repetition, and it cannot be said that such repetition occurs in the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], and His words: ﴿His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. We reply that there, it was good because repeating it indicates that it is the most noble of the types of that universal category, and doing righteous deeds is not the most noble of the types of matters called faith. Therefore this interpretation is refuted. Al-Halimi said: This repetition certainly occurs, because although faith does not include doing righteous deeds, His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ do include faith. So His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ make the mention of His words "those who believe" unnecessary. Also, His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ include His words ﴿and urge one another to truth and urge one another to patience﴾, so that would have to be repetition too. The earlier scholars replied and said: We do not deny that repetition occurs for the sake of emphasis, but the original state is its absence, and this much is sufficient for the argument.

**The second question:** Those who affirm the threat against sinners (the Mu'tazila) argued from this verse. They said: The verse indicates that a human being is in loss absolutely, then He made an exception: ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. What is conditioned on two conditions is absent when either of them is absent. So we know that whoever does not attain faith and righteous deeds must be in loss in this world and in the Hereafter. Since those who combine these two qualities are extremely few, and loss is necessary for whoever does not combine them, the saved are fewer than the lost. Then, even if the saved were more numerous, the fear would be great, so that you would not be among the few. How much more so when the saved are fewer? Should not the fear be even greater?

**The third question:** This exception contains three matters:

The first: It is a consolation to the believer for the loss of his life and youth, because deeds have brought him to something better than his life and youth.

The second: It is an admonition that everything that calls you to obedience to God is righteousness, and everything that distracts you from God toward other things is corruption.

The third: The Mu'tazila said: Calling deeds "righteous" is a sign that the reason for their goodness is not the command, as the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari) say, but rather that the command came because they themselves contain aspects of righteousness. The Ash'ariyya replied: God Most High described them as being righteous, and He did not explain that they are righteous because of aspects returning to them or because of the command.

**The fourth question:** Someone may ask: In the case of loss, He mentioned the judgment and did not mention the cause, while in the case of gain, He mentioned the cause, which is faith and righteous deeds, and did not mention the judgment. What is the difference? We say: He did not mention the cause of loss because loss occurs through an action, which is committing disobedience, and it also occurs through abstention, which is not undertaking obedience. Gain, however, occurs only through action. Therefore He mentioned the cause of gain, which is deeds. There is another aspect: that He, in the case of loss, left it general and did not specify, and in the case of gain, He specified and explained. This is what befits generosity.

*As for His words, Most High: ﴿and urge one another to truth and urge one another to patience﴾.*

Know that when He explained regarding the people of the exception that by their faith and their righteous deeds they had left being in loss and had become people of felicity, in that they held fast to what leads them to attain reward and salvation from punishment, He described them afterwards as having become, because of the intensity of their love for obedience, not limiting themselves to what concerns them alone, but enjoining others with the same way, so that they too would be a cause of others' obedience, as the people of religion ought to be. On this aspect, He Most High said: ﴿O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. So urging one another to truth includes the entirety of religion, both knowledge and practice, and urging one another to patience includes compelling the soul to bear the hardship of the obligation in performing what is required and in avoiding what is forbidden, since undertaking what is disliked and refraining from what is desired are both very difficult. Here there are several questions:

**The first question:** This verse contains a severe warning, because He Most High decreed loss upon all people except whoever brings these four things: faith, righteous deeds, urging one another to truth, and urging one another to patience. This indicates that salvation is conditioned on the totality of these matters, and that just as it is incumbent on the responsible person to achieve what concerns himself, so too are there duties toward others, among them calling to religion, giving sincere counsel, enjoining good and forbidding evil, and wishing for others what one wishes for oneself. Then He repeated "urging one another" so that the first would include calling to God and the second would include steadfastness in it; the first is enjoining good and the second is forbidding evil. From this is His words: ﴿and forbid what is wrong and be patient﴾ [Luqman: 17]. And 'Umar said: May God have mercy on the one who points out my faults to me.

**The second question:** The verse indicates that the truth is heavy, and that trials accompany it, which is why urging one another is joined with it.

**The third question:** He said "and urge one another" (watawasaw) and did not say "and they urge one another" (yatawasawna), lest it be taken as a command; rather, the purpose is to praise them for what proceeded from them in the past, and this indicates their desire to remain steadfast in it in the future.

**The fourth question:** Abu 'Amr recited "bi-al-sabr" (with patience) with a slight rounding of the lips on the letter ba' (bi-shamm al-ba'), a slight element of the vowel that is not fully prolonged. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: This is among the things permitted in pausal (waqf) recitation, and it does not occur in continuous (wasl) recitation except by treating continuation as if it were pause, and this scarcely occurs in recitation. In line with this is what is narrated from Salam ibn al-Mundhir, that he recited "wal-'asir" (by the time) with a kasra on the sad, and perhaps he paused because of breath running short or some obstacle that prevented him from continuing the recitation. In line with this it should be understood, not as treating continuation as pause. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best. May God bless our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
